sourcedFrom: Barrett Model 82A1 Operator's Manual — P/N 82141, REV C (printed on the back cover) (UNDATED — Barrett prints a part number and revision letter rather than a year)
cleanIntro: ⛔ Clean it from the BREECH, every time. Barrett puts that in a boxed CAUTION because a rod entering at the muzzle wears the crown, and on a rifle asked to hold a group at a thousand yards the crown IS the accuracy. The 82A1 comes apart into four groups and a spring, and that is the whole published job. The other thing to get right is what comes OUT before storage: the bore, the chamber and the firing-pin channel go back dry, not oiled.

steps.title: Safety to SAFE, magazine out, then look — the bolt does not hold itself back
steps.action: Put the safety lever on SAFE and press the magazine catch forward to drop the magazine. Then work the charging handle several times and LOOK. On this rifle the bolt does not lock back on an empty magazine, so an empty well tells you nothing about the chamber — Barrett prints that as a WARNING and it is the single most important habit on the gun.
steps.aside: REAR WHEN THE RIFLE OR MAGAZINE IS EMPTY.  ALWAYS PULL THE CHARGING HANDLE TO THE REAR TO INSPECT CHAMBER FOR AMMUNITION.
steps.quote: THE BOLT DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY REMAIN TO THE
steps.cite: Barrett Model 82A1 Operator's Manual — P/N 82141, REV C (printed on the back cover) — UNLOADING AND CLEARING RIFLE

steps.title: Physically check the chamber, not just visually
steps.action: With the muzzle in a safe direction and the safety on SAFE, pull the charging handle to the rear several times and check the chamber both by eye and by finger. A .50 BMG case is big enough to see and big enough to feel; there is no excuse for taking the look on its own.
steps.quote: Clear the firearm by pulling the charging handle to the rear several times; visually and physically check the chamber for ammunition.
steps.cite: Barrett Model 82A1 Operator's Manual — P/N 82141, REV C (printed on the back cover) — UNLOADING AND CLEARING RIFLE

steps.title: Mainspring and buffer: rotate to line the notch on the stop, then let it out
steps.action: Keep constant control and pressure on the buffer and spring, rotate them until the buffer notch lines up with the buffer stop on the lower receiver, then let the spring extend fully before you remove it. Control is the operative word — this is a long spring in a heavy rifle and it will leave the receiver on its own if you let it.
steps.aside: Allow buffer and mainspring to fully extend then remove
steps.quote: While maintaining constant control and pressure, rotate the buffer and spring to align the buffer notch with buffer stop on lower receiver
steps.cite: Barrett Model 82A1 Operator's Manual — P/N 82141, REV C (printed on the back cover) — REMOVING THE MAINSPRING AND BUFFER

steps.title: ⛔ 70 lb of barrel-spring tension lives at the front of the upper
steps.action: Know this before you go near the front of the upper receiver: the barrel springs carry roughly 70 lb (32 kg). Grasp the rear lock pin locked into the barrel key — NOT the springs — when you work them. This is the one place on the rifle where a slip is an injury rather than a scratch.
steps.caution: 70 lbs (32 kg). SERIOUS INJURY COULD RESULT IF SPRINGS ARE SUDDENLY RELEASED
steps.quote: THE TENSION ON THE BARREL SPRINGS IS APPROXIMATELY
steps.cite: Barrett Model 82A1 Operator's Manual — P/N 82141, REV C (printed on the back cover) — ASSEMBLY OF MAJOR COMPONENTS — WARNING

steps.title: Chamber brush, then bore brush — solvent on both
steps.action: Clean after every shooting session, not every few. Solvent on a chamber brush first, then solvent on a bore brush, both worked from the breech. Barrett name their own Heavy Bore Cleaner; what matters is that it is a bore solvent and that the chamber gets its own brush, because a .50 chamber holds more fouling than a bore brush will ever reach.
steps.aside: The rifle should be cleaned and lubricated after each shooting session.
steps.quote: Apply cleaning solvent to a chamber brush and clean the chamber. Barrett Heavy Bore Cleaner is recommended.
steps.cite: Barrett Model 82A1 Operator's Manual — P/N 82141, REV C (printed on the back cover) — CLEANING AND LUBRICATION

steps.title: The muzzle brake gets cleaned WHILE the barrel is wet
steps.action: Do the muzzle brake at the same time as the barrel, with a stiff plastic brush and bore solvent. The reason is practical: the solvent running through the bore softens the carbon on the brake's interior walls, and on a brake this size that carbon sets like enamel if you leave it for another session.
steps.quote: It is best to clean the muzzle brake at the same time the barrel is being cleaned as the bore solvent will help loosen the carbon build-up on its interior walls.
steps.cite: Barrett Model 82A1 Operator's Manual — P/N 82141, REV C (printed on the back cover) — CLEANING AND LUBRICATION

steps.title: Bolt face, extractor and ejector — then test them by hand
steps.action: Bore solvent on the bolt face and a stiff plastic brush into the extractor and the ejector. Then press each one in with your thumb and let it come back. Barrett ask for that test by name, and it is the whole point of cleaning them: an ejector that has gone sticky under carbon is a failure to eject that no amount of solvent on the outside will show you.
steps.quote: Depress the ejector and extractor by hand to test their smooth function.
steps.cite: Barrett Model 82A1 Operator's Manual — P/N 82141, REV C (printed on the back cover) — CLEANING AND LUBRICATION

steps.title: Three named lubrication zones, and nowhere else
steps.action: Barrett name where the oil goes on the 82A1: the upper along the bolt latch trip, and the barrel at the barrel stop and the front barrel bushing; the lower along the bolt carrier rails, the mainspring and the mainspring housing; and the outside of the bolt carrier with the neck of the bolt. Those are the surfaces that slide under recoil — everywhere else oil just collects grit.
steps.aside: Lubricate the exterior surfaces of the bolt carrier and the neck of the bolt
steps.quote: Lubricate the lower receiver along the bolt carrier rails, mainspring, and mainspring housing
steps.cite: Barrett Model 82A1 Operator's Manual — P/N 82141, REV C (printed on the back cover) — CLEANING AND LUBRICATION

steps.title: ⛔ It goes away DRY — and the case goes away dry too
steps.action: Before it goes back in the case: bore, chamber and firing-pin channel free of cleaner, oil and grease. And the case itself has to be moisture-free — a closed case with damp lining is a corrosion chamber wrapped around a rifle that will not be opened again for months.
steps.aside: AND THE INTERIOR OF THE CARRYING CASE SHOULD BE MOISTURE FREE BEFORE THE RIFLE IS PLACED IN THE CARRYING CASE FOR STORAGE.
steps.quote: TO PROTECT THE RIFLE FROM CORROSION, THE RIFLE
steps.cite: Barrett Model 82A1 Operator's Manual — P/N 82141, REV C (printed on the back cover) — GENERAL MAINTENANCE — WARNING

steps.title: Inspect the welds, and the barrel springs, and the brake
steps.action: This is a rifle that recoils harder than anything else you own, and Barrett's inspection list reflects it: check every part for looseness, and check especially along the WELDS for cracks. Then the springs — no gaps between coils when the barrel key is disengaged — and the muzzle brake, which must be tight and fully screwed on.
steps.aside: The barrel springs must not be overstretched, and each coil should be tight, with no spaces between coils when the barrel key is not engaged into the barrel.
steps.quote: Inspect all parts (especially along welds) for cracks or damage and replace, if necessary.
steps.cite: Barrett Model 82A1 Operator's Manual — P/N 82141, REV C (printed on the back cover) — GENERAL MAINTENANCE

steps.title: Ten dummy rounds, by hand, before you believe it
steps.action: Barrett's own function check is a magazine of ten DUMMY rounds cycled by hand through the action, watching them feed, extract and eject. On a rifle where a live function check costs six dollars a pull of the trigger and a shoulder, the dummy-round check is not a nicety.
steps.aside: Manually operate the bolt carrier to the rear and forward, making sure the cartridges feed, extract, and eject properly.
steps.quote: When possible, an operational check using ten dummy rounds should be performed.
steps.cite: Barrett Model 82A1 Operator's Manual — P/N 82141, REV C (printed on the back cover) — GENERAL MAINTENANCE

deepAbsentReason: Barrett publishes no strip past this point for the M82A1, and the book is structured to say so: the rifle's published breakdown is into its FOUR major groups — upper receiver, bolt carrier group, lower receiver and magazine — plus the mainspring and buffer, and after that the manual turns to inspection and troubleshooting rather than further disassembly. There is no published route into the bolt itself, the trigger assembly or the transfer bar; those appear in the GENERAL MAINTENANCE list as surfaces to keep clean and lubricated, and in the exploded view as parts to ORDER, not as parts to take out. ⛔ The one place the book actively warns you away from is the front of the upper receiver, where the barrel springs carry roughly 70 lb — "SERIOUS INJURY COULD RESULT IF SPRINGS ARE SUDDENLY RELEASED". So the deep clean here is the four-group strip in the guided clean above, done properly and often; nothing deeper is presented and none has been invented.

cleaning.name: CHAMBER & BORE
tasks: Chamber brush with solvent, then bore brush with solvent
⛔ From the BREECH — never a rod in through the muzzle
Dry patches until the cleaner is out

cleaning.name: MUZZLE BRAKE
tasks: Stiff plastic brush and bore solvent
Done WHILE the barrel is wet, so the solvent softens the carbon
Checked tight and fully screwed on

cleaning.name: BOLT & BOLT CARRIER
tasks: Bolt face with bore solvent; stiff plastic brush into extractor and ejector
Both pressed by hand afterwards to prove they move freely
Exterior of the carrier and the neck of the bolt lubricated

cleaning.name: RECEIVERS
tasks: Upper: bolt latch trip; barrel at the barrel stop and front barrel bushing
Lower: bolt carrier rails, mainspring, mainspring housing
Everything else: cotton swabs, general-purpose brushes and rags

cleaning.name: ⛔ BEFORE IT GOES AWAY
tasks: Bore, chamber and firing-pin channel DRY
Barrel springs: no gaps between coils with the barrel key disengaged
Rifle AND case moisture-free before the lid closes

reassembly: Barrel rotated so the barrel extension and feed ramp align, then slid forward to the barrel stop.
Impact bumper onto the large diameter of the barrel, against the barrel stop.
⛔ Barrel key worked home by the rear lock pin locked into it — never by grasping the 70 lb springs.
Front barrel bushing mated to the front hinge pin before the upper is lowered — forcing it here damages the rifle.
Charging handle held back so the bolt clears the barrel extension, then released SLOWLY.
Bore and chamber checked dry before any ammunition comes near it.
fncheck: Reassembled and empty: work the charging handle and confirm the bolt runs the full stroke. Load ten DUMMY rounds and cycle them by hand, watching each feed, extract and eject. Confirm the muzzle brake is tight and fully screwed on — ⛔ the rifle must not be fired without it. Then check the bore and chamber are dry.
